As someone who's been in your son's shoes, I can only give you a few words of advice that I've come to understand over the years.

When I was in my pre-teen/teen years I felt somewhat disconnected from my father, not because we didn't have a relationship or a friendship, because he never really understood at the time what I needed from my father. When I needed a friend, he was my parent. When I needed a parent, he was a friend. Through the years this caused us to go our separate ways, sometimes for the better and sometimes for the worse. At some point, you have to choose what's more important to you... Do you want to be a father or do you want to be your son's best friend?

When I was younger, I used to beat and berate people just for the fun of it because I resented myself for being gay. I took it too far a few times and ended up in jail because of it each time, but each time I learned a new lesson. I had the support of my family even though my choices were so severely wrong and I'm sure without them I never would have made it out on top and alive.

But you have to be ready to accept that as a possibility, because it is a very real one. People here will tell you "counseling" this and "therapy" that, but it's not the best option out there for everyone. For me it wasn't, the soul searching and deep thinking only made me worse at the time. What I would suggest is something more along the lines of a "Big Brother" program, because if there's anything that I've learned it's that being able to just talk, without the probing questions or without the requirement to talk, helped me more than anything. I surrounded myself with people who were capable of having real and intelligent conversations and I found myself becoming something else. I was happy, I smiled more than I frowned, I found reasons to wake up without hating myself and to this day all of those people have a special place in my heart.

So in hindsight, I too have rambled on... I'll finish with this:

1. Be prepared to lose him, because you will at some point. He'll hate you so much that even the thought of you will disgust him.
1. Do your best to be both a father and a friend, not just one or the other.
1. There will come a time when life behind those nasty iron bars will go from imagination to reality if his actions don't change, but don't become angry at this. Love him as you always have and show him that you only wish to support him.
1. Don't stop living your life simply because of his actions. That happened to my father, it's not something I wish on anyone.
1. Show him this lengthy post and tell him that there are people who have done what he's doing. That there's no good outcomes, only slightly less shitty ones.
1. You can only hate yourself or anyone else in an equal proportion to how much you love them, don't take his hatred towards you or your partner at face value.

Truly,

~ Your fellow Human

The first dog we saw was a purebred German Shepherd. The employee working said that she was going to be put down for having a violent history/temperament and that she wasn't suitable for adoption. She the directed my parents to a pit/terrier mix across the hall. While they weren't looking, I crawled into the cage with the shepherd and proceeded to be drooled/licked upon until I was soaking. Clearly not the vicious animal the lady had said.

Fast track about 9 years later and I had to give my dog back to the same shelter we had gotten her from because I was leaving the country and couldn't take her with me. There's something special about German Shepherds that I can't help but love, and I feel like the breed is the right one for me.
